game.name: Barony
game.short_description: Barony is the premier first-person roguelike with cooperative play! Adventure alone, or gather a party with iconic and unusual RPG classes to face off against the brutal dungeons. Test your resourcefulness, wits, and friendships, on your quest to lift the evil lich's curse!

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Barony is a first-person, classic dungeon-crawler roguelike with many drastically different classes and a huge amount of content. He finds it deep and potentially great, especially in multiplayer, but very punishing, slow, repetitive early on and confusing for newcomers. He sees why fans love it and says it could be S for them, but it did not click for him personally. He leans to a very high B, possibly A.
praise: Classes play drastically differently (fighter, rogue, alchemist, engineer with robots, spellcaster)
Enormous content and many ways to approach fights and problems, including NPC allies
Rewards learning: a knowledgeable player will have an absolute blast
Likely shines in multiplayer and is a game he would not tire of learning if stuck with one
Emergent, somewhat Dwarf Fortress-like creativity that produces surprising wins
criticism: Insanely punishing: traps and cursed items can kill a long run instantly
Very long runs and slow progression to later floors
Repetitive early floors with the same enemies and items each run
Overwhelming complexity and a gauntlet-like tutorial mansion; needs a beginner's guide
Confusing spell and item handling mid-combat for newcomers
Not satisfying for him: dying suddenly to something not understood and restarting with nothing
unique_points: Tutorial is an entire mansion of hard challenge rooms that many never finish
Mechanically simple combat but very diverse approaches (traps, robots, alchemy, spells, NPCs)
Class variety changes playstyle more than typical roguelikes
commentary.quote: it's going to have to be like a very high B tier potentially an a tier
design_criteria: Class diversity: each class plays drastically differently
Difficulty/punishment: traps and curses cause sudden deaths
Run length: very long runs hurt the feel
Repetition: early floors repeat every run
Complexity/onboarding: steep learning curve and heavy tutorial
Emergent approaches: many ways to solve encounters
Multiplayer potential: likely where the game shines
Content depth: huge amount of things to learn

community.one_liner: A first-person, voxel-style dungeon-crawling roguelike from Turning Wheel with 1-4 player co-op, inspired by NetHack, Ultima Underworld and Hexen-era RPGs.
community.consensus_summary: Barony is well loved by players: Steam shows Very Positive (about 90.7% of roughly 18,200 reviews) and many long-time players with hundreds of hours call it a genre standout, especially in co-op. Critic coverage is thin; OpenCritic lists only two mid-tier critic reviews (7/10 and 7.1/10, averaging 7.05, both for the Switch port) and Metacritic has no Metascore, only a small user score of 7.5 from 45 ratings. The game is still being developed a decade after launch (new DLC and a large systems overhaul), and the most recent wave of negative Steam reviews is largely about that overhaul, not the original design. Common complaints are steep, sometimes unfair difficulty (especially solo), long runs with no meta-progression, and races and classes sold as paid DLC.
best_things: Co-op is the main draw: up to 4 players (online, LAN, split screen), and the party dynamic and class mix is what the game is balanced around
Deep, interlocking NetHack-style systems (item identification, cursed gear, alchemy, skills, magic, traps) that reward accumulated knowledge across runs
High replayability from many classes, races, gear and spells, plus Steam Workshop mods and adjustable difficulty/assist options
Charming retro voxel look, humor (cream pies, chat callouts, RPG-Maker-style sound effects) and a nostalgic Hexen/Heretic feel
Runs on modest hardware, has good controller support and remapping, is DRM-free/open source and runs on Linux
Responsive developers: one reviewer says a dev personally helped fix a startup problem, and content updates have continued for about a decade
Frequent sales make it cheap; many call the base price a good value
worst_things: Brutal early game: instakill boulder traps, swarms of rats and other deaths before players understand what hit them; a steep learning curve and tutorial issues
Best enjoyed in co-op; several reviewers say solo play is very hard and some classes seem designed only for parties
Base game feels stripped: one playable race and about 13 classes, while 13 races and 8 more classes cost extra in DLC (roughly $60 total in one reviewer's math)
Runs are long (multi-hour) and a late death wastes it; no pausing to take a break in multiplayer and hunger keeps ticking
Melee combat is described by some as flat/clunky and loot as underwhelming in early floors, with repetitive locales
Multiplayer desync/lag and crashes at startup or on Steam Deck/Windows are reported by some players
The 2025-26 systems overhaul is heavily criticised by veteran players as slower and less rewarding (see reception_notes)
improvements: Add meta-progression or unlocks so long runs leave something behind; several reviewers call it an arcade score-chaser with no rewards for dying late
Make classes/races unlockable in-game or reduce DLC gating of core content; players also dislike having to beat the game with each race to mix DLC races with classes
Smooth the early game and tutorial, and telegraph hidden traps and instakill threats more fairly
Give players options to keep the pre-overhaul mechanics (lore/identify, swimming, magic progression) rather than telling them to roll back versions
Deepen and polish melee combat and skill variety; some say classes differ only by starting kit
Improve multiplayer stability and add official language support (e.g. Spanish, Russian, Portuguese)
unique_things: One of very few true first-person 3D roguelikes, and with cooperative play without forced PvP; the developer themselves said they rarely see similar games
Combines NetHack-like cryptic item knowledge and permadeath with real-time first-person Ultima Underworld-style dungeon crawling
Proximity-style chat/voice and callouts, enemy chatter and combat music act as gameplay information cues
Open source, DRM free, Linux support, with Steam Workshop mods such as hardcore overhauls
Race and class combinations (including DLC races like salamander or scion with new magic schools) change the playstyle significantly
tedious_or_disliked: Constant defensive play: peeking corners, listening for music and chatter, watching the ceiling for boulder traps
Item identification: the newer Lore skill makes players wait (reportedly minutes) to identify items, and players still have to pick everything up
Being pressured by the Minotaur timer to move faster than a careful style would like
Long, unpausable multiplayer sessions where one mistake can erase hours of progress
Grindy magic progression in the new three-school system, with reaching max in all schools called nearly impossible
Feeling of needing to min-max everything just to survive, and deaths from things you cannot know without prior knowledge
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans say every death teaches you something and it is fair, while others call it punishing in a not-fun way; 'git gud' replies are a recurring complaint from critics
The big systems overhaul and its DLC: some like parts of it, but many long-term players with hundreds of hours gave negative reviews in protest
Price and DLC value: some say it is a steal at sale price, others feel it is a lite base game needing about $60 of content
Whether it is worth playing solo at all versus strictly as a co-op game
community.reception_notes: Released June 2015 on PC (Steam, Mac, Linux; also GOG, Epic and a Switch port) by the small team Turning Wheel. It has stayed a steady seller with a loyal community; Steam Spy estimates 500k-1M owners and a revenue calculator estimates about $3.1M gross (estimates only, not audited). The game has three paid DLCs (Myths & Outcasts, Legends & Pariahs, Deserters & Disciples). Recent Steam reviews show a clear split: a large recent update reworked long-untouched systems (Lore identification, swimming removed, magic split into three schools with level-100 rewards removed, many nerfs) and veteran players wrote protest reviews, some complaining that the developers told them to roll back to an older version rather than add options. Despite this, the overall score remains Very Positive. Because the recent-review sections are based only on a handful of top helpful Steam reviews, the extent of the backlash is not fully measured. No Metascore exists; OpenCritic has only two Switch-era reviews and no aggregate number was found.
